Baruch hadn’t traveled for long before a sign lured him off of the road. It was a weather-worn sign, arrow-shaped and made of knobby-brown wood. The letters engraved on it read “Vitebsk”.

Just the sight of his childhood town’s name reminded Baruch of the spot on the riverbank where he used to sit and learn, the path in the woods where he’d go on long walks with his father, and the fields behind his house where he would chant mishnayos to the tune of the birds. It had been four

years since Baruch had been to any of these places. It was time to visit his hometown.

“Baruch.” Freida grasped the doorpost for support. “Baruch! Come, Kaddish! It’s Baruch!”

Kaddish emerged from the inside room, running as fast as his swollen legs could carry him. Breathless, he stretched out his hand. “Shalom Aleichem!”

politely shook his uncle’s hand and nodded towards his aunt.

Freida shook her head, a dazed look on her face. “Baruch … after all these years … what a handsome young man you’ve become! A beard, and so tall … Now, what was it you asked? Are we well? Yes, yes, Baruch Hashem. But we haven’t been wandering about for the past four years. The question is, how are you?”

Source: Yiddish Memoirs, vol. 1, pp. 79, 88–90 / English Memoirs, vol. 1, pp. 87–88.

LAST TIME: Baruch visits Eliezer Reuven again for Pesach. During Yom Tov, Baruch notices that Eliezer Reuven’s son, Shmuel Nachum, deeply desires to study Torah despite having struggled in school. Baruch encourages Eliezer Reuven to send his son to Yeshiva, and give him another chance to succeed. Coming Back Home

up her palm. “Don’t worry, don’t worry, I won’t force anything out of you. Besides, there’ll be plenty of time for talking now that you’re back with us. Come, let me show you to your room! We haven’t touched it since you’ve left. Oh, you must be so hungry, after all these years—tell me, Kaddish, doesn’t he look thinner?”

“And thinner,” Freida said resolutely. “He looks thinner. You don’t have to worry, Baruch. Now that you’re back here, you’ll have all the food you need.”

Freida led Baruch and Kaddish to the kitchen table, where she set out a bowl of fruit and pitcher of water. Baruch said little, and didn’t touch any of the food or drink.

mostly Freida speaking about how glad she was that Baruch would be coming back to live with them, Baruch cleared his throat and cut in. “I’m just back for a visit. A short visit.”

Freida wagged her index finger.“ You must stay at least long enough to pay a visit to your sister. Devorah Leah, she’s done quite well for herself. She’s married to the most promising young talmid chacham around. Rav Yosef Yitzchak, that’s his name.”

already offered him the job at the yeshiva! Can you imagine, getting an offer so young? That’s our nephew-in-law. You must stay, Baruch, if only to meet him. ”

“Uh…” Baruch stammered. “Devorah Leah. Yosef Yitzchak

and Devorah Leah. I’m sure they will offer to host me, as well, and it would be hard for me to turn them down.”

face fell. “Well, I wouldn’t want to snatch away her guest. Certainly not when it’s her long-lost brother. Well then, you should go already, and say hello to your sister! She’s been worried sick all these years.”

“And your brother-in-law,” Kaddish added. “I think you’d enjoy speaking with him.”

Baruch assured his uncle and aunt that he would visit Devorah Leah, right after he stopped in at the yeshiva. Freida gave Baruch directions to the young couple’s house. Baruch thanked his aunt and uncle, and dutifully promised that he would let them know if Devorah Leah was unable to host him.

Baruch eagerly headed to the main yeshiva in Vitebsk. He came in through the back door and sat quietly on the last bench; he didn’t want to attract too much attention. All he wanted was to hear the shiur of his newfound brother-in-law, and see for himself just whom his sister had married.

Baruch was not disappointed by Yosef Yitzchak’s shiur. What impressed him the most was the colorful crowd: it was a mix of older, learned men, students several years younger than himself, and many ages and stages in between. The shiur was both

stimulating for the scholars and understandable to the younger students. Next, the ga’on Reb Paltiel delivered his own lecture. This one was less well-attended;
